zones.label: Perceivable (P)
zones.summary: Perceivable: Can users perceive the content?
facts: Question: Can users perceive the content?
Example criterion: Non-text content has a text alternative.
Blind learner: Text descriptions of images and a clear heading structure.
Low-vision learner: Strong color contrast and text that enlarges.

zones.label: Operable (O)
zones.summary: Operable: Can users operate the controls?
facts: Question: Can users operate the controls?
Example criterion: All functions work with a keyboard.
Learner who cannot use a mouse: Keyboard navigation.

zones.label: Understandable (U)
facts: Example criterion: The language of the page is identified.
Learner with a reading disability: Clear structure, short paragraphs, and alternative formats.

zones.label: Robust (R)
zones.summary: Robust: Does it work with assistive technology?
facts: Question: Does it work with assistive technology?
Example criterion: Custom controls expose a name and role.
Assistive technology: A name and a role it can read and operate.

quiz.question: Which principle do captions for a deaf learner serve?
quiz.explanation: A user who cannot hear needs another way to perceive the content.

quiz.question: Which principle asks that all functions work with a keyboard?
quiz.explanation: A user who cannot use a mouse must be able to control the page.

quiz.question: Which principle includes identifying the language of the page and keeping paragraphs short?
quiz.explanation: Users can follow a page that is clearly structured and identified.

quiz.question: Which principle says custom controls must expose a name and a role?
quiz.explanation: Assistive technology must be able to read and operate them.

quiz.question: Which principle do strong color contrast and enlargeable text for low vision serve?
quiz.explanation: A user with low vision must be able to see the content.
